findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. They can explain the project after reading it.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: There is a clear next step: a link near the top jumps to concrete instructions (prerequisites, git clone, ./setup.sh, and a first `athena ask "add a changelog"`). The reader knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: This is Athena's site, but nearly the whole page studies a different project, firstmate, in depth. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to scroll past dozens of transition cards and 45 claims that are not about Athena.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; sections States, Counters, Transitions, Claims and sources

findings.text: The page promises a second model that checks the work, costs for each step and a verdict, but none of these appears anywhere on it. The study shows only that Athena can read code. The reader never sees an example of a request turning into a commit.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust, but the prerequisites do not mention a Rust toolchain. A newcomer cannot tell whether setup.sh installs Rust itself or whether they need it already.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: This link sits in the header with no explanation. A first-time reader does not know who the "owner" is or why proposals would be waiting for them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Words like captain, yolo, green, red, home and agent are each defined two or three times. This makes an already long page longer. Defining each word once, with links to that definition, would be easier to read.
findings.source: Headings "Words used first" and "Glossary", plus the "agent"/"code" definitions under Transitions

findings.text: The "Start here" overview already uses exit codes and script internals. That is more detail than a newcomer needs before they understand the basic idea.
findings.source: "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued."

findings.text: This points to an internal folder without saying which repository it is in. A newcomer cannot act on it.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"

findings.text: The page is open about its limits: nothing was run, and an early reading missed some paths. Together with the claim links that point to exact file lines, this makes the study believable.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"
